title: my first PCB design
body:
This was my first complete PCB design project. I followed the hardware design process for an STM32WB Bluetooth Low Energy board and used KiCad to go from a blank project to a board that could eventually be sent to a manufacturer. This is the [tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nkHFoxe0mrU) made by Phil's Lab with 3 parts (Schematic, PCB, Testing). 

I learned a lot from this project, and it was my first time working towards creating a fully functioning PCB from the ground up. Each step in the PCB design process was challenging, brought up circuit fundamentals I've learned in class, and introduced new aspects of design to keep in mind. This took me 3 weeks, or about 5 days of work, to accomplish. 

## 1. Documentation

Before working on the schematic, I went over the MCU (microcontroller unit) [datasheet](https://www.st.com/en/microcontrollers-microprocessors/stm32wb55ce.html) for the STM32WBCE, including application notes and reference designs, to properly implement the unit.

I used the MCU datasheet, ST application notes, reference schematics, and component datasheets to understand things such as:

- which pins needed power
- which pins needed decoupling capacitors
- how the internal power supply circuitry worked
- what crystals were required
- how to connect the Bluetooth RF output
- what external components were recommended

For example, the STM32WB has several power pins and power domains rather than one simple power input. The design tied the required supplies to 3.3 V and placed local capacitors around the MCU according to the intended power connections.

### 1.1 Bluetooth RF

![](/images/uploads/image-13.png)

One example of using the MCU documentation was designing the **Bluetooth RF output**. It contains a reference design on how to implement the Bluetooth antenna. The STM32WB RF pin has to connect to an **impedance-matching network and a low-pass filter** between the MCU and antenna connector.

## 2. Schematic

![](/images/uploads/image-5.png)

The schematic was where the electrical design was created before worrying about the physical PCB.

I started with the STM32WB MCU and added the supporting circuitry around it. This included the power system, clocking, USB, programming/debug connections, and Bluetooth RF section.

### 2.1 Main Components

The **STM32WB microcontroller** is the main device on the board. It runs the firmware and contains the Bluetooth Low Energy functionality.

The **voltage regulator** takes the 5 V coming from USB and converts it into 3.3 V for the MCU and other circuitry.

The **crystal oscillators** provide accurate timing references for the MCU and need to be placed close to the oscillator pins.

The **RF matching network and filter** prepare the Bluetooth signal before it reaches the antenna connector.

The **USB connector** provides both power and USB communication, while the **ESD protection device** helps protect the interface from electrostatic discharge.

The **SWD/debug connection** is used for programming and debugging, while the **UART connection** provides another communication interface during development.

### 2.2 Decoupling Capacitors

A small capacitor is placed next to the MCU power pin to provide a stable current to the overall circuit. As the power source does not provide DC continuously, the capacitors are there to maintain the current. Therefore, smaller capacitors are placed next to the MCU. A larger capacitor was also used as bulk decoupling for the MCU.

The PCB placement matters as much as having the capacitor in the schematic. The capacitors should be physically close to the corresponding power and ground pins(vias) so the current path stays short and low-inductance.

### 2.3 ERC

**Electrical Rules Check** checks the schematic for electrical problems.

# 3. PCB

![](/images/uploads/image-6.png)

PCB design puts an emphasis on component placement, and depending on the importance of a function/signal, we place the components closer to the MCU or the part they directly support.

### 3.1 The Four Layers

Usually, more complex PCB designs require more than 40 layers, as this allows more components to fit within a smaller area and at a greater thickness. 

![image.png](/images/uploads/image-10.png)

Our board uses four copper layers, like this:

```
(Layer 1) F.Cu           - Components
          Prepreg        - Insulation
(Layer 2) ln1.Cu         - GND
          FR-4 Core      - PCB dielectric/material
(Layer 3) In2.Cu         - GND
          Prepreg        - Insulation
(Layer 4) B.Cu           - 3.3V
```

**Layer 1 - F.Cu (components)**

The top layer contains all of the components and important signal routing.

This includes connections around the MCU as well as signals such as USB and RF.

**Layers 2 and 3 - In1.Cu, ln2.Cu (GND)**

The two internal layers are **ground planes**. Current travels down traces and returns to its source.

**F.Cu signals** mainly reference the GND on **In1.Cu**

**B.Cu signals** mainly reference the GND on **In2.Cu**

**Layer 4 -  B.Cu (3.3V distribution)**

The bottom layer is used for additional routing and a large **3.3 V copper pour**.

Vias assigned to the 3.3 V net connect into this copper area, allowing power to be distributed around the PCB without routing a separate long trace to every device.

### 3.2 VRM

The board receives power through USB. Our USB provides 5V to the PCB; however, our components use 3.3V. In this case, we place a VRM (voltage regulator module) next to the USB outlet with input & output capacitors to convert the 5V to 3.3V.

The 3.3 V supply is distributed across the **B.Cu copper pour**. Vias bring that power up to components on F.Cu, while short traces connect the vias to the exact power pins and decoupling capacitors.



Power and ground traces are generally wider because wider copper has lower resistance and lower inductance, resulting in less voltage drop, less unwanted noise, and a lower-impedance path for current.

### 3.3 Vias & Stitching Vias

**Vias** are plated holes that electrically connect copper between PCB layers, either GND or the 3.3V.

Many decoupling capacitors have both a **3.3 V via and a GND via** to keep current connections shorter.

**Stitching vias** connect GND between different PCB layers. They are placed near signal vias to give the signal’s return current a short path when changing layers.

### 3.4 Copper Zones / Polygon Pours

The larger **red/pink filled areas** drawn around sections of the PCB are **copper zones**, also called polygon pours.

Instead of drawing traces between components, a copper zone fills an entire selected region with copper assigned to a specific electrical net.

For example, the internal layers use large copper zones assigned to **GND**, while B.Cu uses a large zone assigned to **3.3 V**. Therefore, our red filled areas are polygon pours used to have that assigned area (components being VRM output, capacitor, and vias) receive 3.3V.

### 3.5 Fiducial Markers

The three small red & purple circles near the edges of the PCB are **fiducial markers**.

Automated assembly machines use cameras to locate these markers and determine the exact position and rotation of the PCB before placing components.

## 4. Traces and Routing

### 4.1 Routing Priority

The most important sections were routed first, including:

- Bluetooth RF
- power circuitry
- USB differential pair
- crystal connections

Lower-speed signals such as GPIO, UART, reset, and LED connections are more forgiving and can be routed afterward.

Routing critical signals first allows them to take the shortest and cleanest paths before the board becomes crowded.

### 4.2 Routing Between Layers

Sometimes there is not enough room to route a signal directly across the top layer, as the traces would cross over each other, and it can't be feasible since each trace runs on its own.

In these cases, they are routed like this:

**F.Cu → via → B.Cu → via → F.Cu**

The first via takes the signal down to the bottom layer, the trace travels underneath the crowded area, and another via brings the signal back up.

### 4.3 USB Differential Pair Routing

USB D+ and D− are routed together as a differential pair.

The tutorial targets approximately **90 Ω differential impedance**.

Both the trace width and spacing between the two traces affect the final impedance.

The traces are kept together and follow similar paths so both signals experience approximately the same electrical environment.

### 4.4 DRC

**Design Rules Check** checks the physical PCB for problems such as incorrect clearances, unconnected nets, and routing-rule violations.

### 4.5 Manufacturing Files

The design is exported into:

```
Gerber files             - each PCB layer
drill files              - define drill vias, holes
Bill of Materials (BOM)  - components, values, PNs, etc.
component-position files - xy position and rotation of each component
manufacturing notes      - other instruction given to the manufacturer 
                          (50ohm RF trace, 90 ohm USB differential pair)
```

The PCB should be designed around these manufacturing capabilities (trace width, spacing, drill/via size, copper thickness, layers) & we should follow this set of limitations to ensure we receive an accurate & working PCB.

## 5. Conclusion

For my first PCB project, I learned a lot. Especially as someone who has never touched on PCB design, this beginner tutorial, although it was challenging, was a great first step for me to understand the process and fundamentals of PCB design. 

I was not able to complete the project to the end with manufacturing and testing/verifying the PCB, but eventually, with my future projects, I hope to do so.
